subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. J. A. DION (LAKE ST. JOHN-ROBERVAL) AND SECONDED BY MR. J. H. DICKEY (HALIFAX)
speechtext:
I wish to refer just for a moment to one passage in the speech from the throne, namely the passage having reference to the question of mutual assistance. The government says it will continue as far as possible to grant mutual assistance but that under present circumstances it does not see how we can continue what we have been doing. Farther on, the text says:
Canada, nevertheless, remains one of the few great producing countries with capacities unimpaired by the war.
The Address-Mr. Bracken

I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that is dangerous talk. In the past we have had dangerous talk, leaving the impression that we were going to have the millennium after the war. That kind of talk is dangerous when we look at the size of our public debt; when we look at the inflation we have in Canada; when we look at the unfavourable trade balance which we have met here now to try to do something about, that unfavourable trade balance with the United States approaching a billion dollars a year. It is dangerous talk in the light of the impending loss of much of our overseas markets, which markets in the past took half of our total exports.
In another place in the speech, it mentions, with respect to price increases, that the government is going to keep them under constant supervision. What that means I do not know. Presumably the government once kept under constant supervision the price of milk, the price of bread, the price of vegetables, and the price of automobiles. And yet those prices have all gone up and will go up higher under the government's present policies.
I mention these things only to point out this. If we do not get more production and retain more of it, these prices will continue to go up; because the money is there to buy it, unless the government takes it away from us by taxes or by loans. The only way in which we can correct this inflationary condition is to get more production; and, having obtained more production, then to see that enough of it is left in this country so that prices will not go up.
The other day the Prime Minister mentioned that there were about four or five measures that the government wished to have dealt with at this session. The particular measures were the Geneva trade agreements; the so-called emergency measures-more properly I would say the totalitarian powers measures; also the taxation measures; and then two measures already in effect which will terminate at the end of this year just because we happen to meet here this year. They would have lasted until March 31 if we had met after the end of this year. The government wants them extended.
. Let me refer very briefly to one or two of these and at greater length to the others. With regard to the transitional measures act, as I said, they would have been in effect until March 31 in any event if we had not met now. It was debated last year. There is no time now to discuss that measure. I suggest that there be discussed among the members the attitude they will take on it. We shall be opposed to much that is in it, but since it is only an interim measure, since it was passed
fMr. Bracken.]
before and since it will come up for discussion next year anyway, it is possible that it might be dispensed with after only a short debate. In any event, I want to say to the government that we are prepared to help them see that it is dealt with one way or another before we leave here this month.
With respect to the Agricultural Products Act, which is another act that terminates this year only because we are here in December and not in January, we shall want to ask some questions about it. We are concerned with respect to the future trade with Britain. We have been concerned, as I am sure the government must be concerned, because it has not been able to fill its contracts. Only a very small proportion of the contracts has been filled, in some cases. We want to know what the real situation is with respect to markets over there for hogs, cattle, cheese, eggs and other farm products.
I now come to what the government chooses to call its emergency legislation. My criticisms of the government's policies in this respect I shall state only briefly at this time. I will elaborate on them when I have stated them. We criticize the government first for delay in attacking this problem; a delay which has multiplied many times the severity of the problem; a delay which we say is inexcusable. We criticize them for the procedure they took to bring some of these measures into effect. We say they were an insult to parliament. We say they were brought into effect behind closed doors under a piece of legislation that the government itself told us it would not use for that purpose. We criticize the government also for trying to drag in an issue which has no relationship at all to this immediate problem; that is, the question of the Geneva agreements. That was dragged in to give a better appearance to the government's real' policies; dragged in to confuse the public with respect to the emergency parcel the government had decided to hand the country.
Now let me deal with these things one at a time, first with the delay. It is appropriate to inquire whether November 17 was the earliest possible day at which the government could have been aware of a problem of such gravity as to require the attention of parliament at a special session. For a few moments let me examine the record of events to see whether prior to that day, there was any evidence of Canada's critical condition. I have taken from the records a great deal of evidence to show the government had ample warning of the condition which was facing us.

The Address-Mr. Bracken
Here is one dated February 8, 1946, coming from the governor of the Bank of Canada, who said:
The prevailing optimism on the North American continent is dangerous if it diverts attention from the problems which have to be faced ... It seems likely that there will be far greater delayed reactions from world war II than from world war I, unless positive steps are taken to prevent this.
Again I quote from the same gentleman, under date of February 11, 1947:
It is normal for Canada to have a deficit in its current account balance of payments with the United States, and this deficit is likely to average higher in the future than it has in the past . . . Our imports from the United States in the fourth quarter of 1946 were about $430 million as compared with less than $500 million in the whole year 19.37, and less than $900 million in the whole year 1929.
That is from the governor of our own Bank of Canada. In April of this year the Economist, a distinguished authority in the United Kingdom on economics and finance, pointed out that Canada's position in regard to United States dollar reserves was almost identical with that of Great Britain. I could go on; I have a dozen or more of these warnings as to what was impending, but I need mention only a few of them. On April 17, in a dispatch from Ottawa, the Financial Post said:
The blackest possible picture of an approaching dollar crisis for the whole world has been painted here in Ottawa in the last few days by officials of the British 'treasury.
I need not take the time of the house to read all these warnings; those I have given indicate what most students of this question knew. On September 4, Australia found it necessary to cut her imports of Canadian newsprint by thirty per cent because of the dollar shortage.
In view of the evident lack of action, I then asked the government to call a special session of parliament to consider the obviously grave situation.
On September 8, New Zealand announced restriction on all imports from Canada except essentials, and on the same date Ceylon announced similar restrictions; yet there was no word from this government as to what was likely to be done. On October 8, I appealed to the Prime Minister, and I quote my words-
-as one Canadian to another, to forget party advantage and to concentrate upon the future welfare of this country; to call a conference of the commonwealth governments to devise plans for meeting the dollar crisis which we share in common.
The result was deep silence. The record goes on to show our reserves getting lower
month by month as we went along. At last, at very long last, the government admitted what the rest of the nation had known for months; that is, that a very grave situation faced Canada and that prompt, effective action was necessary. No longer could the government pretend that they alone belonged upon Olympus, or that they alone were endowed with superior wisdom and knowledge, or that they knew there was no danger and no need for action. The record of the warnings the government had is appalling; the warnings were constantly repeated; the facts were incontrovertible. The failure of the government week after week and month after month to take any action whatever has cost the nation hundreds of millions of dollars of its reserves and has doubled, trebled and even quadrupled the severity of the measures it is now necessary to take. Britain took action weeks before the Geneva agreements were signed. France did not wait, nor did Australia, New Zealand or Ceylon. But Canada did wait.
I need not take time to answer some of the excuses the government has given; there will be opportunities for that later on. Why was there this delay? Why the failure to act when the situation so clearly and imperatively demanded action? Why all this added cost to the nation? Why the long delay necessitating action so severe as that now being taken? I give the answer. It was because the government thought it politically expedient. The issue was before us. The government thought it saw an opportunity to excuse itself before the people of Canada by waiting until the trade agreements were announced, thinking it could confuse the issue in that way. The government delayed because it sought to hide the wolf of economic necessity in the sheepskin of the Geneva agreements. The government was willing to sacrifice the interests of the nation in order to protect its party from the . mounting criticism. The government delayed because it regarded political advantage to its party as more important than the welfare of the nation. The government in this matter stands revealed for what it is, insincere as well as incompetent.
I come now to the procedure followed by the government in dealing with this matter. They have used the powers conferred by the Foreign Exchange Control Act. I now refer to Hansard for August 9, 1946, at page 4530. where the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said:
This is not an attempt to restrict trade between the two countries; it is just 'the reverse. This is a measure intended to assist trade.

The Address-Mr. Bracken
And further along on the same page:
I repeat that the whole purpose of the measure is to provide for the- efficient handling and conservation of our essential foreign exchange resources.
Then the predecessor (Mr. Ilsley) of the present minister had this to say, at page 2547 of Hansard for June 17, 1946:
We have no intention of using this exchange control legislation to restrict anything but certain types of capital movement.
Then a little further on:
It is for this reason that it is necessary to maintain our over-all machinery for control even though our intention is to place no restrictions on current account transactions.
I now come to what their experts told us in the standing committee on banking and commerce. The record is all here,.but I shall take only a few typical statements. I quote from page 10 of the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee last year:
Q. There would be the danger that funds might be dissipated by bringing in what you call non-essentials?
This is the answer by Mr. Rasminsky:
What would be necessary in that contingency, Mr. Queleh, would be for the government of the day to take appropriate action other than through the foreign exchange control board to limit our expenditure of United States funds for such purposes.
And a little farther down-and I will not take time to quote all these, but will refer to only a few-Mr. Rasminsky says:
I think the answer to that is that the ordinary legislative process would be at hand. If the government found it necessary to restrict imports from the United States because we are running short of American funds it would have the same courses of action open to it as were open to it and as it took in 1940, namely to introduce a measure into parliament to provide for the restrictions that were necessary. That is, as regards the import of goods, this act ensures-if I may say so-against bureaucratic control over the import of goods; it ensures that if it becomes necessary to take that measure it will be the legislature which takes it.
Then another quotation from another answer:
The foreign exchange control board has nothing whatever to do with the types or the quantities of goods which are imported into Canada or exported from Canada.
And a little farther down, Mr. Rasminsky says, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore):
The answer is that if circumstances arose in which for one reason or another it seems desirable to place restrictions on the import of goods into Canada, then it is evidently the opinion of the government in this measure that the
fMr. Bracken.]
power to place those restrictions, should not be conferred upon an administrative body such as the foreign exchange control board.
That is the kind of impression the house was given as to the purpose of the measure, and for what it was to be used. Then, I read the following question by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming):
In other words, the suggestion there is no regulatory power vested in the board with reference to imports, at the expense of any power parliament now has in that regard, Mr. 'Rasminsky, was referring to the export and import of goods rather than securities and currency?
The answer was, "That is right".
Those are typicai of the views given to us by ministers of the crown and by experts in their employ as to the purpose of the act and how the government intended to interpret it. In spite of all that, they came along a month or two ago and used that act to do the very thing for which they said they would not use it.
I now come to my criticism of what the Prime Minister calls his short-term policy. But, sir, the government's sins are not alone those of omission. There are many sins of commission also for which they must answer. Most notable of these is their re-valuation of the Canadian dollar in July of 1946. The government artificially re-valued the Canadian dollar, raised it from ninety cents where it had been for years, to SI. This step was taken in defiance of the fact that the scales of Canadian-American trade were so heavily tipped in America's favour that the Canadian dollar situation did not warrant and could not support any theoretical parity.
The unfavourable effect of this re-valuation was immediate and overwhelming. Our unfavourable balance of trade rose from $5-5 million in 1945 to S525 million in 1946, and to $587 million in the first seven months of 1947. Let me say at once that the first figure I gave was one respecting an unusual year; that was not the normal state of unbalance. The figures just prior to that were around $300 million or $400 million a year.
Then came, as a result of the government's decision, the drying up of our American dollar income. The flow of United States capital investment in Canada then proceeding at a rate of nearly $300 million annually completely dried up. Only a trickle remained. Finally, Americans began to take advantage of an exchange position which they realized could not last. As a result, the loss on our balance of payments

that is, the export of gold and American dollars-rose in 1946 and the first half of 1947 to ten times the loss experienced in 1945.

The Address-Mr. Bracken
The ill effects of the government's action soon appeared in our domestic industry. In our gold mining industry, for example, production fell off to less than one-half that of the pre-war period. This was particularly serious because gold is the one commodity for which the United States maintains an unlimited market. Without our gold production, our trade deficit with the United States-and I would ask hon. members to take careful note of this figure-without our gold production our trade deficit with the United States would have been increased by 82,349,000,000 in the twenty-two year period 1926-1947. Yet this industry has been crippled by government policy.
Nor was the gold mining industry the only one placed in difficulties by the government's unwise policy. Our largest export industry, that of pulp and paper, found it impossible to continue selling in the United States market at the old price. Successive increases in price were necessary. This rise in the Canadian price level made it possible for Canada's competitors, notably the Scandinavian countries, to re-enter that market, and this year Sweden will sell to America approximately ten times the paper she sold there in the previous year. Nor is that all; the cost of Canadian paper, it is held by some authorities, is now approaching such a high price level as will make it economically feasible for Americans to process their fat pine of the vast forests of the southern states, thus permanently restricting Canada's largest single export.
Mr. Speaker, I now come to a consideration of what the government proposes to do. I come to the kernel of the government's short-term programme. The government has floundered into such a morass that only the most drastic action can retrieve our position. The Progressive Conservative party will not oppose any measure which gives hope of effective relief in these dire conditions into which the government has blundered. We object, however, to the term "austerity programme." The government cannot by attaching that phrase to its programme bask in the reflected courage of the British people.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. J. A. DION (LAKE ST. JOHN-ROBERVAL) AND SECONDED BY MR. J. H. DICKEY (HALIFAX)
speechtext:
The Canadian government's policy is a programme of totalitarian dictatorship. They pose as the great party of freedom; they pose as the great party of free trade. But as the government's good friend, the Winnipeg Free Press pointed out on November 26, the government's policy is one of super-protection. That is not my word; it is the word of the government's greatest newspaper friend in western Canada.
I come now to the question of embargoes. The first of the government's cure-alls are the import controls. Much of their benefit has been lost through the long delay which enabled United States businessmen to pour their goods into Canada, even by diversions from their own domestic market in some instances. The embargoes necessarily are more far-reaching than would have been the case had action been taken earlier. The government now says it has no alternative, that we must accept the restrictions. This, however, does not excuse the government for attempting to blame the people of Canada for the buying spree in the United States. When the government sets up conditions that favour buying in another country, manipulates its currency to facilitate that buying, and then does not even inform the people of the seriousness of the situation, then the government cannot shift one iota of the blame to the people. And the attempt to do so is cowardly.
Talk about a spending spree! When the government itself gives a lead in curtailing wasteful and extravagant spending it will be time enough for the government to censure the people of Canada for buying goods in the United States.
Just a word now about these new excise taxes. The new excise taxes are another of the government's remedies. They are to fall upon Canadian produced goods and upon British imported goods quite as much as upon United States goods. Their sole effect is to raise costs, to raise prices and to stimulate further the inflation which the government says it does not want. In our judgment, these measures serve no useful purpose; they will do much harm. We do not think they should be continued. So far as the government has proposed tax relief with respect to sugar, tea, coffee and so on, naturally they will have our support. However, we want to hear from the Minister of Finance with respect to the taxes they are imposing and why he thinks they are necessary. We will determine our course in the light of the argument he gives, but at the moment we are disposed to oppose these taxes.
Then with respect to the gold subsidy, it seems that the government has a positive genius for finding the worst possible way to do anything. One could wish that it would devote half of the energy which it puts into doing things the wrong way into finding the right way once in a while. Nowhere is this more clearly exemplified than in the case of the gold subsidy. Everyone is aware of the plight of the gold industry, of the fact that it is able to produce less than half of the gold it was producing five or six years ago.
The Address-Mr. Bracken

This industry produces the one commodity which can be exchanged without limit for United States dollars. But what does the government do? It sets up a scheme which will do either one, or both, of two evil things. Either the entire energy of the industry is to be diverted into new development, a procedure which will require imported equipment that the government has now banned; either there must be new developments which will produce no gold for two or three years, or the established mines will have to concentrate on their high grade ore, thus exhausting it prematurely and at great waste. If the present policy is continued much longer the gold industry of this country will be crushed out of existence. They are carrying on now only because the men in their employ are willing on account of the economic squeeze they are in, to take less than other men in similar callings just in order to have their jobs. As I say, if these policies are continued this industry will be destroyed. Today it is producing only half of what it did a few years ago.
Responsible men cannot countenance such false methods. We are against the gold subsidy as it now stands. There can be no justification in Canada for having two prices for the same commodity, for having this man getting $35 an ounce and that man getting $42 an ounce. Either there should be a free market for gold or, if it is to be subsidized, the subsidy should be industry wide. It should be fair to all and it should be sufficient to get out the gold.
I come now to what is perhaps the most objectionable feature of the government's policy. I come now to the crowning folly of the government's short-term scheme-the arbitrary powers given to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe). This can be characterized only as the restoration of the great despotism. For years during the war this country lived under the arbitrary rule of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. I want to pay him the highest compliment for his work during the war. For years business, industry and the individual have been subjected to the arbitrary decree of ministerial discretion and secret decisions carried out 'by order in council. We were told during the war that it was necessary for us to be deprived temporarily of our liberties in order that we might enjoy them in security in peacetime.
Now that we are in peacetime, we are informed that we are to continue to live subject to arbitrary government and personal whim instead of by the due process of law and the judgment of the courts. Every Canadian was endowed at birth with the inalienable rights and privileges which are the heritage of
IMr. Bracken.]
British people everywhere. If these unparalleled restrictions are necessary in this emergency, and they well may be, then let them be embodied in detail in an act of parliament which can be debated by the representatives of the people in the proper democratic tradition, and let the statute be enforced in the impartial courts according to our immemorial custom. Well might that great jurist, Lord Hewart, refer to the new despotism of irresponsible authority. We have felt its heavy hand and we want no more of it. Naturally we shall oppose the bestowal of such arbitrary power upon any man or any group of men.
I come now to the Geneva trade agreements, the trade agreements which, as I said the other day, have been dragged in here to give a semblance of respectability to the government's other proceedings, or to confuse the public with respect to the other policies which the government is bringing in. The government did not need to bring this measure before the house at this time. It did not need to do that except for the purposes I have indicated, to confuse the Canadian people, to get them thinking about these things when the real issues are the immediate issues with which I have been dealing.
Section 11 of the tariff act reads as follows:
The governor in council may by order in council make such reductions of duties on goods imported into Canada from any other country or countries as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for reductions on Canadian products granted by any such country or countries.
That is the law. It has been there for many years. It enables the government by order in council to make reductions in tariffs by agreements with other countries. It has been used at least twice, once in 1935 and once in 1938. I hold in my hand a copy of the Canada-United States and the United Kingdom-United States trade agreements. Here is what happened. Those agreements were entered into and there was no special session called to deal with them. Members were not called in from all across Canada to talk about them and deal with them. What happened? The agreements were signed on November 17, 1938, and the rates were to be provisionally in force on January 1, 1939.
That is something like what is happening in the present agreements. I repeat that the agreements were signed on November 17 and the rates were provisionally in force on January 1. No special session was called. Parliament was called on January 12 of the next year, 1939. On that date the agreement was tabled. The resolution was introduced on February 11, and on March 9 the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe moved that the agreement be

The Address-Mr. Bracken
referred to the committee of ways and means. On March 29 the resolution was reported and the bill introduced. It received second reading and the next day it received third reading. The legislation was passed four months after the agreements had been made.
That could have been done today with these agreements. There was no need to bring us here to talk about these agreements. They have very little if anything to do with the immediate question; they have been dragged in here for some reason which the government can try to make clear, if it can.
I can summarize now the position we take with respect to some of these things that have happened. The parliament of Canada has been brought into special session to consider a grave economic crisis in the history of the nation. I indict the government on the following counts:
1.	The government has been wilfully negligent of the public interest. It has let this crisis develop, in fact helped it to develop. It has delayed action and then deliberately set out to confuse the issue in the minds of the public.
2.	The government has carried out ill-conceived and hastily prepared stop-gap measures which have worked great harm and will continue to work great harm to the nation.
3.	The government has resorted to arbitrary and tyrannical methods, in an attempt to overcome its past mistakes.
4.	This is perhaps the most serious of all. The government is rapidly losing our overseas markets, markets which, as I indicated a little while ago, have been for decades the market for half of our exports.
I suggest, sir, that on these four grounds alone-and there are many others-the government stands condemned before this house and before this nation.
What are the alternatives? I think the government is wrong in approaching this problem entirely from a restrictionist and a scarcity basis. That is what all these measures mean. We should still consider all means of solving it on an expansionist basis. All embargoes on our goods entering the United States should be withdrawn. Let us keep in mind that the over-all problem which is pushing us into a severe programme of austerity is the scarcity of United States dollars. And in the face of that the government has been refusing our farmers the right to send products over there to get United States dollars. The government by its action hindered the increased production of our gold mines to get United States dollars. I was in British Columbia the other day. A man met me and said, "I am in the lumber business. I cut telephone poles. I cannot sell them where I am here in Canada, but the government will not allow me to sell them in the United States." That is the kind of thing we are up against. And when they changed the value of the dollar they ruined our tourist business.

speechtext: I am very glad the leader of the opposition is more courteous than some of his supporters. My question is, does my hon. friend think for one second that this suggested policy will injure the lumber business of British Columbia?

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. J. A. DION (LAKE ST. JOHN-ROBERVAL) AND SECONDED BY MR. J. H. DICKEY (HALIFAX)
speechtext:
I can only tell the house what this man said. He said, "I have carloads of telephone poles. I cannot sell them here and I am denied a market across the border." I am giving the minister the man's own words. He is in the lumber business.
As I said, let us keep in mind that the overall problem which is pushing us into a severe programme of austerity is the scarcity of United States dollars. We shall get United States dollars only if we sell our goods over there; we shall never get them by selling only at home. We are prepared to support gifts to Britain or loans to Britain, but it is absurd to be carrying on a lend-lease system with the British on our own, and then going on bended knee to the United States to get help ourselves. It is not realistic and it does not make sense. I would therefore remove the embargoes and permit our products to go into the United States and reap United States dollars as they do so. I suggest to my hon. friend who just asked me a question that he read the account in the paper which supports his party day in and day out in the city of Winnipeg, the Winnipeg Free Press. It will tell him whether the government's new policies are in the interests of Canada or not.

Secondly, I would take full advantage at once of any reduced duties that are provided in the agreements; that is, [DOT] any that are not nullified by the action the government took the same day that they announced these agreements. They said, here are great agreements to expand trade. But then the modem Jeremiah came along and said, "We are not going to expand trade; we are going to prevent trade." I would take full advantage of the reduced duties that are
The Address-Mr. Bracken

provided in the agreements. These will be made effective by the President of the United States as of January 1 next.
Thirdly, I would correct the mistake that was made on July 5, 1946, when the value of the dollar was altered arbitrarily by this government. Great damage has been done since then, damage caused by that very act. The drain of dollars has been so great that the amount of depreciation permitted within the Bretton Woods agreement would not be sufficient to cure the worsened situation, but it would do something.
Fourthly, if we must temporarily restrict imports let the government come to us with a list of those restrictions, place them in an act of parliament and reserve the powers of making laws to parliament. Do not place the power to make tariff laws in the hands of a minister and a body of bureaucrats. We still believe in government by law rather than government by decrees dictated by czars. The men who will gain most are those who will have the smoothest trail to the minister's back door.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. J. A. DION (LAKE ST. JOHN-ROBERVAL) AND SECONDED BY MR. J. H. DICKEY (HALIFAX)
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will pardon me, perhaps he will allow me to' speak along lines which are more agreeable to him, as they are to myself.
In the first place I should like to join with him in very warmly congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am sure it has been a pleasure to all members of the house to listen to the two addresses we have had this evening. It is a pleasure and satisfaction for many reasons. It must be apparent to all who have heard the mover and seconder, that we have in their persons valuable additions to the membership of this house. The hon. member for Lake St. John-Roberval (Mr. Dion) came into the house at the last general election. He has spoken very seldom thus far, but this evening he has shown us by his free delivery and carefully thought out arguments that he possesses the qualities which are so essential in making a good parliamentarian. I should like to extend the warmest congratulations to him on the manner in which, in what he has said, he has represented his constituency and in what, by way of example, he has contributed to debating in this house.
It will be observed in regard to both speakers that in some particulars they have had a similar training and possess a similar

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
background. Each is a lawyer who has a high standing in his profession. Each is a war veteran, which is a qualification of exceptional merit for any member of parliament to possess at this time. And as we have seen this evening, each is capable of addressing this House of Commons in both the English and the French language. That again is perhaps as helpful a qualification as a member of parliament in our country can possess. I do congratulate most warmly the mover of this address.
Now I say to the seconder of the address, mv hon. friend who has just come into the house from Halifax, we all appreciate the difficulty one experiences in making a maiden speech. Some of us have heard many maiden speeches in this house in the course of the years we have been members of it, but I am sure it will be agreed that no member of the house has acquitted himself more admirably in his maiden speech than has the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) this evening. Like the hon. member for Lake St. John-Roberval (Mr. Dion), he has had important legal experience. He has dealt with some important national and international problems; and already, though he is comparatively young in years, he enjoys a reputation as a public speaker and as a sound thinker which few men of this country have enjoyed at his age.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is encouraging to all of us to observe the type of men who are coming into this house at this time. Having regard to the ability which they are showing at so early an age in their careers, one, who, in the course of a short while, may be passing from the scene altogether, will be able to look back with confidence to those who are following on, realizing that our country will be safe under their guidance and direction. I for one am particularly happy that, in the addresses to which we have listened to-night, we should have had anew an assurance that Canada's younger men may be trusted to carry out the ever-increasing responsibilities which those who govern in this country will have to assume during the years to come.
Now may I thank my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, and also the mover and seconder of the address, for the kind references they have made to the honour recently graciously conferred upon myself by the King. The pleasure derived from this royal recognition will always be the greater in that it has been so cordially received by my fellow citizens. May I say to this parliament that I am deeply grateful that, through the leader
of the opposition tonight and those who sit around him, all hon. members have been kind enough to cause me to feel that they too approve the award made by His Majesty.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition asked me if I would say something about my recent trip abroad, to touch upon what I had thought and observed in the course of that sojourn. It is perhaps best to begin by referring to the trip itself and the reason for it. I was invited by His Majesty to be present as the representative of Canada at the royal wedding. A more exceptional opportunity to visit Britain could hardly have been presented to anyone. Among the special honours and privileges of the visit was that of presenting in person to Her Royal Highness the Princess Elizabeth the gift from the people of Canada. I think hon. members are already aware of the nature of the gift. In deciding upon a gift for Her Royal Highness, it was not an easy matter for the administration to hope to satisfy everyone; and it was very difficult indeed to know what would be the most suitable gift to make. Fortunately, we had in the Princess Alice, Countess of Athlone, a lady in whose good judgment we knew all Canadians had confidence, and one who, we felt, would be able to assist the government materially in the selection of a suitable gift. We accordingly asked Her Royal Highness if she would lend the government her good offices in making the selection, and endeavour to ascertain from the royal family what gift would likely be most acceptable to the Princess herself. I may say we felt that the most suitable gift would be one the bride herself would wish to have; we ascertained through Princess Alice that what Her Royal Highness would really like would be silver for a table service which would be of assistance in entertaining and in carrying out some of the duties she and her husband would have to discharge later on. Her Royal Highness expressed a preference for pieces of antique silver. The government had very little doubt as to the wisdom of the choice; and we left it with Her Royal Highness Princess Alice to make the selection, within limits which were indicated. I should mention also that we felt a gift which would be especially welcome, in a very personal way, would be a mink coat. This was added to the gift originally chosen.
I want to convey to members of the house, and through this house to the country, the very warm thanks of Her Royal Highness Princess Elizabeth for the gift which came to her from Canada. Her Royal Highness expressed with real delight her appreciation of the gift, and asked if, upon my return, I would convey her thanks, as probably she herself

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
will do later on in a written communication, to the government and the people of Canada. I might add that the gift from Canada seems to have given great pleasure not merely to the princess but also to Their Majesties and to Her Majesty Queen Mary. One of the great pleasures afforded by my recent visit to England was the opportunity to renew friendships with Their Majesties, who have so great an attachment for Canada and who spoke at length of their visit here, and also to meet again Queen Mary, one of the greatest women in the world today.
I should say also that I extended to Her Royal Highness and the Duke of Edinburgh a very warm invitation to visit Canada at an early date. This I did not only on behalf of the government but also on behalf of His Excellency the Governor General and Lady Alexander. I was warmly thanked for the invitation, but a definite acceptance has not been given up to the present, and I imagine we shall have to wait a little time before we know when it will be possible for the visit ;o be made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
I thought a very full account had already appeared in the press, together with pictures. The gift consisted of candelabra, of salvers, of plates, and generally a service for a large table for purposes of entertainment, all of antique silver. I shall endeavour to see that photographs of the gift appear in the press so that hon. members and the people of Canada may have some appreciation of the nature and beauty of the gift.
When it was announced in the press that I would be visiting England for the wedding, I received an invitation from the government of Holland to pay a visit to the Netherlands. I also received a similar invitation from the Prime Minister of Belgium, and shortly before leaving I received a communication from the President of the French Republic inviting mo to meet His Excellency and some of his ministers at luncheon on the day of my arrival in France I mention these invitations, as hon. members will be quick to recognize, not as having been extended to me personally, but as invitations extended to me as the representative of the people of Canada to whom the countries mentioned wished to give expression of their continued admiration and gratitude. Unfortunately the ship on which I crossed was a day late in arriving and I was unable to keep the invitation of the President of France. The day following, however, I had

the honour of meeting the then Prime Minister of France, Mr. Ramadier, and having with him a conversation of some length. In the evening I had the honour of being the guest of Mr. Bidault, the foreign minister, and met with him a number of other members of the government of France. I mention these receptions as they will enable hon. members to see the opportunities there were of gaining in a very short time first-hand information in relation to some of the conditions to which I shall make reference a little later on.
The visit to Paris, of course, was very short, but during that visit it was possible to gain some very denite impressions. The visit to Belgium, though fortunately longer, was similar in its nature, in that the Prime Minister invited me to be his guest and meet his colleagues. I also had the honour of meeting His Royal Highness Prince Charles, the Prince Regent of Belgium, together with a number of members of parliament and the Speakers and some of the members of both houses.
In the Netherlands, I had a similar opportunity of meeting the Prime Minister and his colleagues on different occasions, and of renewing a personal friendship with Her Royal Highness Princess Juliana, at the time the Princess Regent of the Netherlands, who became so well known to many of us in Canada during the. several years she resided in the capital of Canada. I also had the honour of meeting anew Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands. Her Majesty wished me to renew her expression of thanks to the people of this country for what our armed forces had achieved in liberating the Netherlands.
I have made reference to the warmth of the welcome extended by these several countries. The warmth of that welcome; its many manifestations; the honours which came from the heads of governments, from parliaments, from universities, from municipalities and organizations, one and all, were intended as expressions of admiration and gratitude to the people of Canada, for our country's part in helping to liberate the nations of northwestern Europe during the period of the great war, and what has since been done to help them in assisting in the work of recovery. I do not believe it would be possible for anyone who did not actually have an opportunity of visiting these countries to begin to appreciate how deeply in mind and heart these peoples cherish the remembrance of all that has been done for them by Canada, and the gratitude they feel for what Canada stands for in the world today, particularly in relation to the solution of many of the problems they have been facing.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
Nothing could have expressed more clearly the high place Canada holds in the regard of the governments and peoples of these countries than these several manifestations. And may I hasten to say that, at base, the gratitude is primarily for and due to the tremendous sacrifices made by members of Canada's armed forces in helping to liberate the countries in which they fougnt in the recent war. Nothing could touch the heart of a Canadian more in visiting the Netherlands than to see the cemeteries in which thousands of Canadian youths still with us until a year or two ago are having their last long rest. The same is true in Belgium and Erance of many who fought and died in the first world war. It must be a comfort to those who have lost relatives overseas to realize that the peoples of Belgium and Holland, where these cemeteries are located, are giving so much personal attention and exceptional care to the graves of their loved ones. The same will be found to be true of burial grounds in France. That is but one of many manifestations of a feeling which lies much too deep for words on the part of the citizens of these countries. I hope all of us will realize that, while the war has Drought terrific sacrifices in every way, nevertheless since the war, and as a result of what happened during wartime, there has grown up between the peoples of these countries and our own country what amounts to a feeling almost of kinship. It seems to me that is one of the great assets we now possess as we face the terrible situations which confront certain parts of Europe, and which may come to affect a very large portion of mankind.
Nations which fought together for liberty cannot bind themselves too closely to each other; we cannot bind ourselves too closely together as a means at this time of helping to continue to preserve liberty.
Just one further thought I should like to mention in this connection. I refer to our national anthem. When one is abroad, one experiences a double feeling of pride as one hears "O Canada" as well as "God Save the King" being played along with the national anthem of the country he may happen to be visiting. I felt an emotion greater than that I had experienced at any other similar time when I heard the playing of our "O Canada" at the same time as other anthems were played, as people stood bare-headed in reverence and recognition of our land. Also, the words of "O Canada" will ever have for me an entirely different meaning, or at least a supplementary meaning to that which they held formerly, after having listened to them being sung in other countries. The words of
"0 Canada" had been learned and were sung by choirs as a special tribute in one or two of the countries I visited. When we sing "0 Canada" we sing the words, "We stand on guard for thee." And, indeed, we do stand on guard for Canada, as our own country. But when one hears a great body of men and women in a country like the Netherlands sing "0 Canada, we stand on guard for thee," the significance of those words becomes more profound and deeper than they otherwise could possibly be.
I shall say only a word about the conditions in those countries so far as one could learn of them in so short a time. I would hesitate even to pretend to say anything about conditions, had I not had the opportunities I have mentioned, and had I not received a good deal by way of what one would regard as inside information-I might call it more accurately authoritative information-in regard to what is taking place at the present time.
From reading the press, I believe hon. members will have learned how deplorable conditions in France have become within the recent past, a condition which no doubt is due in part to the suffering of the people which has not yet been relieved, but which, I believe, is due in larger part to communistic influences which have been fomenting trouble and which, unless they cap be checked, will help to undermine the progress and security of that nation.
I wish to be guarded in my observations. I have no desire to add anything to the alarm which now exists; but I would say that, at the present time, I imagine nothing is occasioning more concern to the people of other countries, as well as to the people of France, than the very unsettled condition in France and in one or two other countries to which, later, I may refer briefly.
Let me speak about Belgium. A visit to that country today would perhaps disclose conditions more prosperous than one might imagine they could be. There can be no doubt that the people of that country have made a marvelous recovery in many directions. If there were no cloud overhanging their borders, and if they were not threatened with penetration from within by subversive forces, I believe it would be no time at all before Belgium would find herself pretty much where she was before the war.
There is this to be remembered when one observes conditions in countries like Belgium and Holland: They were occupied countries, just as France was an occupied country. For that reason they did not suffer, except in some places, to anything like the extent of a country like Great Britain which was not



The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
occupied, but which was bombed continuously from day to day over a period of years.
At times that fact may be lost sight of. There is still, however enough damage in cities such as Antwerp in Belgium and Rotterdam in the Netherlands to make it necessary for time to play its part in helping to restore the damage done to those countries during the war.
I would say at this point that the people of the Netherlands have reason to feel happy, as they do, that their country has recovered to the extent it has. I believe they would be the first to say, in that connection, that they owe to Canada a debt which they will never find it possible to pay. They have not forgotten that it was Canadian troops which freed their country from the oppressor and gave its citizens the opportunity to go again on their way as a free people.
To one who has had the opportunity, as I have had, to visit the United Kingdom on three or four occasions since the war, the fact becomes manifest that the British people are determined to restore the damage done by war as rapidly as possible and are meeting the situation with the greatest fortitude. In outward appearance London shows improvement on each succeeding visit. The same is true of the people one meets on the street. But one must continually remember that poverty hides its head, and misery does not appear in high places. Behind these outward appearances of improvement there can be no doubt that the great mass of the people are suffering from privation and from lack of food and, like other countries, that Great Britain is being held back by lack of materials. Having regard to what the people of the United Kingdom went through during years of war, and the years which have succeeded it, any assistance that can be given is something which cannot be considered too carefully.
The wedding was a bright spot in a very dark sky. For a moment it seemed to give the British public a chance to feel that old times were returning, and the people enjoyed a day of national rejoicing. May I say here what I said when leaving London, that, if there had been no cloud over the skies of Europe, I would have returned from Great Britain realizing that, while there is great privation and suffering there, nevertheless the people are determined to see and would find that in the course of time they will come back to the position they occupied some years ago. But again there are menacing clouds upon the horizon. I wish to say to this House of Commons that the cloud of uncertainty that is over the world today is something that is-1

might use this word-appalling. I do not believe it is possible to exaggerate what may come at this time or almost at any moment as a result of the conditions that exist in Europe at present.
I want to be very careful in what I say because I realize how serious the situation is and I should not like to exaggerate its seriousness in any way. We have at the present time, as hon. members know, the council of foreign ministers meeting in London. Thus far they have not been successful in getting very far toward agreement in the making of peace with Austria or Germany. Every one is asking himself today when searching his own heart. "What is to happen if that effort does not meet with success at this time?"
No one can say what may happen, but there are significent words that have been used within the past few days of which I think this House of Commons should take note. They are deeply significant. It is by such phrases perhaps, that one is able to judge just how serious the situation may be. I should like to draw attention to one word of the secretary of state for foreign affairs in England. This may have been noticed by some hon. members, but it may have escaped the notice of others. I should like to quote a passage that appeared in the press of November 29, in a dispatch from London as follows:
Russian Foreign Minister V. M. Molotov challenged the United States, Great Britain and France to deny that they had plans for setting up a separate German government in the western zones if the current London meeting of the big four fails. British Foreign Secretary Ernest Bevin replied to Molotov that he had never made such a statement but added "if the settlement of the peace is to be blocked we can't continue with chaos. If peace is to be denied we cannot be expected to stand by inactive."
Then within the past day the secretary of state of the United States made another significant statement. It is but one of many, but I should like to place it beside the quotation I have just given. This is a Canadian Press dispatch from London dated December 4. It reads:
Marshall and Molotov traded direct verbal blows for the first time in the present foreign ministers meeting, conference officials reported.
The American state secretary, his ire aroused by Molotov's charges that the other powers were trying to "enslave" Austria, indirectly referred to the Marshall programme and declared Molotov was trying to wreck it.
These are the words of Secretary of State Marshall:
"We are all aware of the real purpose of attacks of this nature," Marshall said. "It is to disrupt the great cooperative movement that is being launched for the economic recovery of Europe."

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
It seems to me that in those two statements hon. members have something which will enable them to get a picture of what is happening or developing in a large way at this time. The impression seems to be that Russia is aiming at a centralized government in Germany, one government which will have control of the whole of Germany, but which, according to the views of many, would be directed from Moscow, and that if she does not succeed in getting that, in having that aim met, we may have again a long period in which no peace settlement can be made with respect to Austria and Germany.
Then there is the impression that everything is being done that can be done to foment unrest, particularly in western Europe, and to make it impossible for the Marshall plan to succeed. In other words, it is felt that this is part of the deliberate policy of communism as it is being spread throughout Europe at this time, that there must be such unrest stirred up in all countries as to make it impossible for a settlement to be reached at the present time. There seems to be little doubt in the minds of those who are close to the matter that if western Europe cannot be saved from the appalling position in which it is at the present time, if there are to continue to be millions of people with insufficient food and clothing, if there is to continue to be social unrest fomented from underground sources, the whole continent may get more or less out of hand altogether.
I do not wish to say more at the present time. I think I have said sufficient to indicate that I believe there has not been a time, except prior to the recent war, when matters were shaping in such a threatening manner as they are at the present time. While it is difficult to suggest what can be done to meet the situation, perhaps the first step in that direction is to realize, that the situation is indeed a very serious one. I shall not say more on that at this time; I may have occasion later on to speak of it again.
Hon. members are, I think well aware that the Marxist theory is that there is inevitable conflict between communism and capitalism. That is where the hopelessness, in some ways, of this situation lies. The Russians appear to believe, or at least their leaders assert that, in order to save itself, capitalism will sooner or later turn upon Russia because she is the communist centre, that therefore they must be continually protecting themselves, that therefore they must have their satellite nations 5849-5
serving as a curtain along their frontiers in order to protect their people. That is on the one side.
On the other side you have the belief that, because of the doctrine of the class struggle being in the minds of the Russians the only means of solving the problems of today, that the development of the totalitarian state is the settled objective of the communist party wherever it is operating throughout the world; that it is being directed from the one particular centre, and that that is a situation which it is very difficult indeed to control.
I ask hon. members to look at the world as it is at the moment. First, go to the far east and see the condition that is threatening there. I ask them to look at Asia where today there is still actual fighting. Then come to the middle east where the threat of war is on the horizon at the moment. Then come to a country like Greece where you have a condition of unrest and strife that is extraordinarily difficult to control. Take next the position of France, Austria and Italy and consider the social problems they are facing and the unrest that exists in those countries. Wherever one looks, there are today on the horizon problems that are baffling the best minds of our day.
I hope I shall not be misunderstood if I say that our country does stand high in the eyes of other nations. We have seen the kind of thing that has taken place in the chamber of deputies in France within the last few days; we have seen the kind of thing that has taken place in the assembly in Italy and in legislatures of other countries. I believe that one of the torches we can hold high in the world at this moment is to keep this parliament a model assembly, illustrating to the world how democracy can be Carried on by argument and persuasion rather than by a course of procedure which is certain to create a wrong impression.
I believe, in my heart, that the greatest service men and women can render today- and this is about the only service that many individuals are in a position to render-is that of preserving, as far as they can toward everyone., an attitude of good will, of doing what they can to remove ill will which, so far as the human mind is concerned, is as contagious, in its way, as disease may be with regard to the human body. We are not going to solve any problem in this world today by any magical formula. They will be solved only if each individual does his part and each

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
nation does its part to help to the utmost to further the common good of all, by a right attitude toward all.
I have not much time before it will be eleven o'clock. My hon. friend will perhaps excuse me, therefore, if I do not attempt to reply at this time to much of what he said. The greater part of my hon. friend's remarks this evening was taken up in discussing the Geneva agreements and also the so-called emergency measures. These are both items which are on the programme and which will be discussed in considerable part during the next two weeks. Therefore, I think I need not go into the points he has raised tonight, but will leave it to the course of the debate on these questions to develop the replies to him by other ministers, if not by myself, and by the discussion on the floor of the house.
However mistrustful hon. gentlemen may be of the government's intention in bringing these two groups of measures down at this time, I can say to this house quite honestly, knowing the situation as I have from the beginning, that we were deeply concerned about the loss of United States dollars over quite a period, but we were informed by those who were concerned with the Geneva negotiations that that conference had a great possibility of succeeding; and that it would be unfortunate if anything were done in Canada which would prejudice the success of the discussions that were taking place there. That was the reason we waited until we knew definitely that the final agreement had been reached before we took the step to call parliament and to have those great questions discussed here.
May I say that I cannot agree with my hon. friend when he says that the emergency measures are more important than the larger question. Both are questions of trade, and we shall find increasingly that our problems of an emergency character are going to be effectively solved only as the problems of trade as they affect the entire world are brought to a successful solution.
No country in the world is as much dependent as Canada is upon foreign markets, and the development of this nation, as my hon. friend knows very well, lies in our having the largest possible measure of opportunity to trade with other countries of the world. The Geneva agreement is something that has not been equalled at any time in negotiations between nations in the way of freeing the barriers of trade and restrictions as between different nations. It is a great triumph; and it is right that the people of Canada, when they are discussing these emergency measures which are unpleasant, which are the last thing in the world that this government would wish

to bring down at this time, should fully realize that they are temporary measures. They are not permanent measures; they are not protectionist measures in any sense of the word. They are sharp for the reason that we hope they will be effective. We hope that their duration will be the shorter, because they are sharp. It is out of the prosperity that we have had in this country that this situation has arisen. If our people had not been' making and spending the money they have they would not have been purchasing to the extent they have in the United States, particularly great quantities of luxuries. I will not go into that question tonight, but the government wants the people of Canada to understand that these emergency measures are temporary in character. The people must not be blind to the larger opportunities that are going to come out of the Geneva agreements as a consequence of the agreement that was reached there.
My hon. friend spoke about this being an emergency session!

speechtext:
With regard to the question of bringing them up now, the government felt that when the agreement was signed we should be prepared to accept it and we ought to put it into force at the time that was provided, but that parliament should know about it immediately and should approve it

____________The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
as soon as possible. We also felt that the emergency measures should be brought forward to be dealt with. We could not undertake them earlier, because to have done so would have interfered with negotiations at Geneva. As my hon. friend well knows, we had to put the emergency measures into force at the moment we did, and not wait any longer because of the fact that otherwise, as in the case of the budget resolutions, all kinds of advantage would have been taken by those who wish to profiteer and those who wish to benefit from changes that were to come about.
My hon. friend spoke of this as an emergency session. This is not an emergency session. We carefully considered that very point. The government might have had an emergency session to deal with these questions only, but we felt that the people of Canada and hon. members themselves would much prefer to begin the regular session now. Let us get that much further ahead, if we can, with the business and spare the country the cost of an extra session and spare hon. members the necessity of coming to attend a special session. This is the regular session of parliament for the balance of the present year and for the coming year.
My hon. friend spoke about the speech from the throne. He said that there was not much in it. He said that he had heard many speeches from the throne and this had less in it than any other. I hope he will not mind my saying that I have heard many speeches by leaders of the opposition, but I never heard as long a one with as little in it as I have heard tonight.
My hon. friend christened the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) Jeremiah. I think he said that Jeremiah was the author of Lamentations. May I say to him, if he digs a little deeper into the source of the Scriptures and becomes more accurate, he will probably discover that leading authorities
claim that Jeremiah had nothing to do with writing Lamentations; the Book of Lamentations was written by half a dozen different poets and authors whose combined efforts were brought together in Lamentations. I would say to my hon. friend that, be that as it may, there can be no denying that his speech tonight was a Jeremiah from one end to the other. If there ever was a weeping political Jeremiah, I think he would merit that title after his address tonight.
My hon. friend spoke about other issues. I see it is eleven o'clock and I will simply say this. He referred to the rising cost of living in this country. Yes, undoubtedly the cost of living is rising and it is a real problem, but may I say that in that regard he will search the world over before he will find another country that is as fortunate as ours.
Iu regard to strikes, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has brought out this evening, we have fewer strikes in Canada today than there are in any other country.
The question of primary industries and the like brings us to another field, to which we arc going to give fuller attention later. As it Is now almost eleven o'clock I will not delay the house any longer. I will give my hon. friend the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) the assurance that a continuance of the present debate will come first on the order of business tomorrow; that he will be afforded the right to speak first, to be followed by the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low), with a reply to be made by some hon. member from this side, after which the government intend to proceed with the introduction of the resolution respecting the Geneva agreements.
On motion of Mr. Coldwell the debate was adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
